summary.name: SRE at Google: SLOs, SLIs, SLAs
summary.one_liner: A Google Cloud blog post from the CRE "life lessons" series explaining how SLIs, SLOs and SLAs are defined, why they matter, and how Google distinguishes them.
use_cases: Deciding a reliability target for a new service
Explaining the difference between an SLA and an SLO to stakeholders
Measuring service availability from successful and failed queries
Setting contractual uptime commitments with refunds
Deciding whether to add redundancy or planned downtime
summary.what_it_does: The post defines a Service Level Objective (SLO) as a numerical availability target and a Service Level Indicator (SLI) as the direct measurement used to check it, such as the frequency of successful probes. It explains why an SLO is needed, arguing that without one a team has no principled way to judge acceptable downtime. It describes how an SLA is usually looser than the internal SLO and carries penalties such as partial refunds. It also covers measurement pitfalls, such as excluding out-of-quota responses and counting only legitimate queries. The post closes with a summary of principles, including defining reliability, measuring success rates, and setting the lowest reliability you can get away with.
notable: Explains the SLA vs SLO distinction with a worked Shakespeare search API example including refund tiers
Covers the idea that an SLO that is too high becomes the expectation, and Google's quarterly planned-downtime exercise for internal front-ends
Shows how to account for bad client traffic and quota misconfigurations when computing SLA success rates
caveats: This is a blog essay on concepts, not a software tool; it provides no implementation or code.
The worked numbers are illustrative examples from the post, not general guidance.
